units.text: Non-Abelian Vector Dark Matter and Lepton g − 2
I. INTRODUCTION

The existence of dark matter (DM) [1,2] is a one of the prevailing puzzles in particle physics. One of the most favored approaches to this problem exploits the fact that Weakly Interacting Massive Particles (WIMPs) in thermal equilibrium produce the dark matter relic abundance in the correct ballpark. The most successful theory in particle physics, the Standard Model (SM) is devoid of any DM candidate 1 . In this work, we explore the possibility of extending the SM with SU (2) X gauge symmetry and consider non-Abelian vector bosons to be the WIMPs. In this framework, the SM leptons, both lefthanded and right-handed ones transform non-trivially under SU (2) X , which plays, among others, a significant role in obtaining the correct relic abundance via dark matter annihilation into SM leptons. Since SM leptons are charged under SU (2) X , new fermions must be added for gauge anomaly cancellation.

A model where only the SM left-handed leptons are charged under extended SU (2) sector is proposed in Ref. [5]. The possibility of neutral vector boson as dark matter candidate arising from this type of SU (2) sector has been considered in Refs. [6][7][8] 2 . In addition to lefthanded ones, right-handed SM leptons can also transform non-trivially under the added SU (2) group, as suggested in Ref. [10]. In this latter set-up, neutral vector boson remains a possible dark matter candidate and such a scenario is studied in Ref. [11].

Besides dark matter, the SM is currently under scrutiny due to the precise measurement of the muon anomalous magnetic moment (AMM) a µ , which is extremely sensitive to physics beyond the SM (BSM). There has been a longstanding tension between the theoretical prediction and the value measured at the BNL E821 experiment [12]. The recently announced result of FNAL E989 experiment [13], which has a smaller uncertainty, is fully compatible with the previous best measurement. A combined result of these two experiments shows a remarkably large deviation of 4.2σ with respect to the SM prediction [14]. Various BSM scenarios are proposed to explain the observed significant departure, for a most recent review see Ref. [15].

In addition to the muon AMM, the electron AMM a e is also measured in the experiments with unprecedented level of accuracy. The recent improved measurement [16] of the fine-structure constant using Caesium atom shows a smaller value for a e with 2.4σ confidence level 3 compared to theory value [18]. The deviation ∆a = a exp − a SM is positive for the muon, whereas, it is negative for the electron. Moreover, the ratio ∆a e /∆a µ is somewhat larger in magnitude than the naive leptonmass-scaling m 2 e /m 2 µ , which evidently makes it challenging to explain both these deviations concomitantly 4 .

Since the DM candidate non-trivially interacts with the lepton sector, the framework we consider in this work, namely, the neutral SU (2) X extension of the SM, it is then tempting to propose a combined explanation of all aforementioned puzzles. Hence the philosophy of our work is to postulate that the new physics (NP) contributions to the muon and the electron AMMs are intimately related to the origin of DM. II. MODEL

Gauge group and Fermion fields.-We consider a framework where the SM is supplemented by SU (2) X gauge group and consider the possibility that both the left-handed and right-handed leptons are charged under it [10,11]. This requires additional fermions to cancel gauge anomalies and an anomaly free set of fermions (per generation) is given below:

SU (3) c × SU (2) L × U (1) Y × SU (2) X are presented.

To generate masses of the BSM fermions, SU (2) X must be spontaneously broken. The simplest possibility is to consider a SM singlet, which transforms as a doublet of SU (2) X that we denote by φ = (φ 1 , φ 2 ) T ∼ (1, 1, 0, 2). The SU (2) X gauge symmetry can be completely broken by the VEV φ 1 = v X , which subsequently generates vectorlike masses for the BSM fermions E, E and N, N (except the right-handed neutrinos ν R ).

As usual, the SM symmetry is broken by the Higgs doublet, H = H + , H 0 T ∼ (1, 2, 1/2, 1) that acquires the usual VEV H = v = 174 GeV. All of the SM fermions, including neutrinos receive Dirac type masses as a result of EW breaking. Breaking of the EW symmetry allows a mixing between the E and E states (and similarly for N and N states), which turns out to be crucial to provide significant contribution to lepton AMMs to be discussed later in the text.

A spectacular feature of this model is that when the SU (2) X local symmetry is spontaneously broken, a residual global U (1) symmetry emerges from it [11]. Looking at all the interactions of this theory, viz, Eqs. (6), (10), and (18), it is clear that all the SM fermions along with right-handed neutrino ν R , the BSM neutral Higgs φ X , and Z are neutral under this U (1), whereas E, E , N, N , and the vector boson X † , each carry one unit of dark charge Q X = +1. We identify this as the dark U (1) X symmetry, which is responsible for stabilizing the dark matter in our set-up. In this work, we consider a scenario where the gauge boson X is the dark matter candidate, hence must be the lightest among {E, E , N, N , X}.

It is to be notated that in this theory the SM gauge bosons receive additional interactions that can potentially affect the EW precision data. Consequences of these interactions are discussed in Sec. IV.

IV. EXPERIMENTAL CONSTRAINTS
Here we summarize relevant experimental constraints of our model.

LHC constraints.-The large hadron collider (LHC) is searching for charged fermions beyond the SM. For each flavor, we have two types of singly charged fermions that we commonly denote as F ± = E ± , E ± . Even though our BSM fermion F ± has no interactions with quarks, they can still be pair produced at LHC via schannel γ/Z exchange as displayed in Fig. 3. This Feynman diagram shows that once produced, each F ± will decay into a dark matter (lighter than F ± in our scenario) and a SM charged lepton that gives rise to pp → − + + / E T . Processes of this type are constrained by LHC due to the standard slepton searches [64][65][66]. Assuming the existence of both the left-handed and righthanded partners, as in our case, LHC puts a lower limit of 450 GeV for their masses [65]. LEP constraints.-In addition to dark vector boson, since our model also contains a Z that does not carry any dark charge, it directly decays to SM leptons as de-picted in Eq. (18) (the first term). Processes like this are highly constrained by LEP experiment [67]. In fact there are two types of Z searches, indirect and direct, and the former seems to provide stronger bound in our scenario. Direct bound is applicable for Z mass below the center of mass scale of LEP-II that constraints m Z ≤ 209 GeV. On the other hand, indirect bound arises from four fermi contact interaction leading to e + e − → f f originating from integrating out Z (f is any SM fermion). The strongest bound comes from e + e − → + − final states, which for vectorial coupling corresponds to Λ + − V V = 24.6 TeV [68]. Following the analysis performed in Ref. V. DARK MATTER RELIC DENSITY AND DIRECT DETECTION

Dark Matter Parameter Space.-As already mentioned in section II, the single-charged BSM fermions, E, E and the neutral fermions, N , N , and X † carry the conserved dark charge, Q X = 1, and compose the dark sector of this model. We consider X to be the vector dark matter candidate 6 in this work, and to avoid its decay into the BSM fermions and charged leptons, l and neutrinos ν l , X → E l, E l, N ν l , N ν l , the mass of X is set to M X < m E,E , m N,N . Dark Matter Relic Density-The relic abundance of X is achieved via standard thermal freeze-out mechanism. The 2 → 2 (co)annihilation channels that give dominant contributions to the freeze-out of the nonrelativistic X are,

• X X † → Z Z annihilation channel that involves 4-point interaction, the exchange of X in t and u channels and the exchange of φ X and h in the s-channel. As this annihilation mode consists of massive vector bosons in both initial and final states, the comparatively large multiplicities in this channel will lead to a larger cross-section. On the other hand, if the low-velocity approximation, σv = a + b v 2 , is used to calculate the relic density, this annihilation channel turns out to be forbidden, which is not the case during the thermal freeze-out since it occurs at the temperature around T f ∼ M X /30 − M X /20, and the energy of the DM follows the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, as pointed out in [80]. As a result, this annihilation mode largely determines the relic abundance of the vector DM, X.

• Apart from Z Z in the final states, one can also have X X † → Z φ X , and Z h i.e a vector boson and either the BSM neutral Higgs (when M X > m φ X ) or the SM higgs boson in the final state. This annihilation can proceed through the exchange of Z in the s channel and the exchange of X at t and u channels.

• X X † → ll, ν l ν l , i.e. to the SM charged lepton pairs and neutrino pairs (l = e, µ is the lepton flavor index) via the exchange of E, E and N, N , respectively, in the t-channel and the exchange of Z , φ X and h in the s channel.

• X X † → φ X φ X , φ X h, and h h i.e. annihilating into the pair of BSM neutral Higgs bosons and the SM Higgs bosons, and into one heavy Higgs and one SM Higgs bosons via the 4-point interaction, the exchange of X in the t and u channels and the exchange of φ X and h in the s channel.
Besides, the additional channels that participate in the coannihilation are,
• X E, X E → ψψ , X N, X N → ψψ and their charge conjugated channels.
• E E, E E , E E → ψ ψ and N N, N N , N N → ψ ψ and their charge conjugated channels.

Because of large number of final states for these coannihilation channels, for simplicity we denote all of the allowed final states using ψ ψ where any one or both of ψ, ψ either indicate the SM particles or the particles carrying zero dark charge, i.e. Z and φ X depending on kinematic conditions. We calculate the relic abundance of X using Mi-crOMEGAS v 5.2 [81] in which we implement the model with the help of FeynRules [82]. For such small θ, the annihilation channels that contain the interaction vertices with the SM Higgs and the dark sector particles, and vertices with the BSM neutral Higgs and the SM particles, will give negligible contribution to thermal freeze-out of the DM, X. VI. RESULTS

In search of finding a valid point in agreement with LEP as well as LHC limits, we perform a χ 2 analysis. In this numerical procedure, we minimize the function χ 2 = i P 2 i , where the pull is defined as P i = (T i − E i )/σ i . For an observable i, T i , E i , and σ i denote theory prediction, experimental central value, and experimental 1σ uncertainty, respectively. The sum is taken over i = {∆a e , ∆a µ , ∆T, Ω.h 2 }. This is a constrained optimization that includes the experimental constraints implemented on top of χ 2 -function. The best-fit point obtained in this procedure leads to ∆a µ = 1.5 × 10 −9 , which corresponds to a pull of P = −1.69 (χ 2 total = 3.8). For rest of the observables pulls are smaller than unity. This best-fit point is allowed by all bounds arising from current experiments, as can be seen from Fig. 5 (point marked as red star; for this best-fit M X /(g X /2) = 7.19 TeV > Λ LEP ). Despite of satisfying LEP bound, since the muon AMM cannot be fitted within its 1σ range, we conclude that this model disfavors a simultaneous explanation of both the muon and the electron g − 2. VII. CONCLUSION

In this work, we have presented a model that sheds light on the origin of the dark matter and also resolves tantalizing anomaly observed in the muon anomalous magnetic moment. The proposed framework extends the SM by SU (2) X gauge symmetry, under which SM leptons transform non-trivially. The new gauge bosons that play the role of dark matter, with the help of additional fermions needed for anomaly cancellation, furnish prescribed quantum corrections towards the lepton anomalous magnetic moments. When contemporary collider constraints and EW precision measurements are taken into consideration, we find that simultaneous explanation of the muon and the electron AMMs along with obtaining right DM relic abundance is highly disfavored. This leads us to a specific scenario for which only the muon is charged under the added SU (2) X . In such a scenario, our analysis shows that a viable parameter space of the model for which the new gauge coupling is g X ∼ 0.2 − 0.8 and DM mass is M X ∼ 0.5 − 2 TeV can explain dark matter relic abundance as well as the large deviation observed in the muon g − 2, recently confirmed by the FNAL result.
